newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bourse pressures firms to adopt merger code.
newsitem.headline: German bourse pressures firms to adopt merger code.

text.p: Germany's bourse, Deutsche Boerse AG, launched an aggressive campaign for its takeover code on Monday, warning that firms which did not accept the voluntary code could be refused inclusion in German stock indices.
Werner Seifert, its chief executive, made the thinly-veiled threat at a news conference to announce the listing of ProSieben AG -- the first German television broadcaster to list its shares.
"We intend in the future only to admit a company to one of our indices when it has already agreed to abide by the takeover code," Seifert said.
"I would encourage you (ProSieben) to do this," he added.
Inclusion in the major bourse indices -- the DAX-30 and DAX-100 -- generally boosts turnover and liquidity in a stock, making it more attractive to investors.

Germany introduced the voluntary takeover code in October 1995, calling on companies to pledge to stand by its rules. But the code has so far found the support of only 270 of a total of 683 listed companies.
Of the top 100 firms in the DAX-100, just 61 have pledged to abide by the bourse's rules.

Under the terms of the gentlemen's agreement, a company which owns a stake of more than 50 percent in a target company is required to make an offer to outstanding shareholders, except in instances where an exemption has been granted.
The company has 18 months to make an offer, although the rules indicate that the price should be near to market levels at the time the offer is made.
Exemptions could be made when the company is an approved majority shareholder and is accepted as such by the target company's annual shareholder meeting.

The code in many ways resembles Britain's well-established takeover and mergers agreement, which is also not legally binding. But the British version calls for an offer at an earlier level, once a stake reaches 30 percent.
Linking the code specifically to ProSieben, Seifert told the news conference: "There is no doubt that your (ProSieben's) capital structure protects you against a takeover.

"But perhaps you yourselves will want to make your business group more valuable and efficacious in the future via acquisitions....We continue to be of the view that a voluntary pledge to abide by this code is preferable to a legal ruling."
Germany hopes its action on takeovers will prevent Brussels from drawing up European merger laws, which it warns could be much tougher than the German model.

The voluntary takeover code is intended to create greater transparency in the German market, which is so riddled with cross-shareholdings and merger defences that it has been nicknamed "Fortress Germany" by foreign predators.
This tightly-meshed network of industrial holdings means most takeovers here are friendly, family affairs.
Earlier this year, when Fried Krupp AG Hoesch Krupp made an apparently hostile bid for Thyssen AG, the attack ended in a friendly agreement to merge their two steel companies.

And in one of the most spectacular cases of an external hostile bid in recent years, Italian tyremaker Pirelli AG finally had to abandon its bid to acquire Continental AG after running into takeover barriers and the closed ranks of banks and industry.

For years Germany also insisted that its gentlemen's agreement to prevent insider trading was fully adequate. But it moved in late 1993 to introduce legislation against insider trading which threatened offenders with fines and imprisonment.
